brief: String of '#' (mine), digits 0-2 and '?'; each digit must equal the number of mines among its two neighbours. Count fillings of '?' that satisfy all digits (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: Scan left to right with 3 states: cell is a mine / digit that needs a mine next / digit that forbids a mine next.
solution: 1. States after cell i: s0 = cell i is a mine, s1 = digit whose right neighbour MUST be a mine, s2 = digit whose right neighbour must NOT be a mine. 2. Start with s0=0, s1=1, s2=1 (virtual left border: not a mine, next cell unconstrained). 3. Place a mine (char '#' or '?'): allowed from s0 or s1 -> new s0 += s0+s1. 4. Place digit d (char d or '?', d in 0..2): allowed from s0 or s2; left=(came from s0); need=d-left must be 0 or 1; need=1 -> s1, need=0 -> s2. 5. Answer = s0 + s2 at the end (s1 would need a mine past the end).

brief: Edit distance S->T where each insert/delete shifts all later characters by 13 (mod 26); find minimum operations. Exact twist is uncertain (garbled source).
key_idea: Shift by 13 twice is identity, so only the parity of insert/delete count so far matters: dp[i][j][p].
solution: 1. Statement is too garbled to fix the exact rule; likely model: dp[i][j][p] = min ops having consumed i chars of S and j of T, p = parity of insert+delete ops so far. 2. Current S char seen as (S[i]+13p) mod 26. 3. Match/replace: dp[i+1][j+1][p] from dp[i][j][p] with cost 0 if shifted S[i]==T[j] else 1. 4. Delete S[i]: dp[i+1][j][p^1] +1; insert T[j]: dp[i][j+1][p^1] +1. 5. Answer min over p of dp[n][m][p]. Confirm the exact shift rule before using.

brief: Array with costs X (subtract 1 from every element of a chosen subarray) and Y (set one positive element to 0); find min total cost to make all elements zero.
key_idea: Divide and conquer like CF 448C: for a positive segment, either zero each element (Y each) or subtract its minimum with X-ops and recurse on the pieces.
solution: 1. f(l,r,base): segment of elements all > base (current already-subtracted amount base). 2. Option A: zero every element of the segment individually: Y * (r-l+1). 3. Option B: subtract the segment minimum m with subarray ops: X*(m-base), then split the segment at elements equal to m and add f on each piece with base=m. 4. f = min(A,B); answer = sum of f over maximal positive segments with base 0 (this is CF 448C Painting Fence with costs). 5. Use a sparse table for range-min to make each call cheap; worst case O(n^2) recursion depth handled by small n or iterative stack.
complexity: O(n^2) worst case time, O(n) space (O(n log n) typical)

brief: Count ways to cut array A into contiguous segments so that the product of every segment has at least X divisors (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: Divisor count of a product only grows when a segment is extended, so for each right end r the valid starts are l <= L(r) with L(r) non-decreasing; dp with prefix sums.
solution: 1. Factor each A[i] with a smallest-prime-factor sieve. 2. Window [l..r] keeps prime exponents; divisor count d = prod(e+1); keep log(d)=sum log(e+1) as a double to avoid overflow (compare with log X - 1e-9). 3. For each r: add A[r]; while l<r and window [l+1..r] still has >= X divisors, remove A[l], l++. If [l..r] has >= X divisors then L(r)=l else no valid start. 4. dp[0]=1, dp[r] = P[L(r)-1] where P is prefix sum of dp (segment starts at any l' <= L(r)). 5. Answer dp[n] mod 1e9+7.
complexity: O(N log A) time, O(A) space for the sieve

brief: Split array into contiguous pieces of length <= M minimizing the sum of bitwise ORs of the pieces; print mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: For a fixed right end there are at most ~31 distinct OR values over all starts; for each value-block take the min dp over the allowed start range with a range-min segment tree.
solution: 1. dp[i] = min over start s in [i-M+1, i] of dp[s-1] + OR(a[s..i]); dp[0]=0. 2. Maintain list of (orValue, smallest start) for subarrays ending at i: OR every entry with a[i], add (a[i], i), merge equal values keeping the smaller start. 3. Entries sorted by start descending; entry k covers starts [l_k, l_{k-1}-1] (entry 0 up to i). Clip to s >= i-M+1. 4. For each block query min dp[s-1] over the clipped range (segment tree over dp, filled as computed). 5. Sum fits in long long (<=1e14); print dp[n] % 1e9+7.
complexity: O(N * 31 * log N) time, O(N) space

brief: Delete at most k characters from a string to minimize the length of its run-length encoding (like LeetCode 1531 String Compression II).
key_idea: dp[i][k] over suffixes: either delete s[i], or make s[i] the start of a run and choose which later chars to keep in that run.
solution: 1. Assumed LC 1531 version: encoded run of length c costs 1 + (c>1) + (c>=10) + (c>=100). 2. dp[i][k] = min encoded length of s[i..] with k deletions left; dp[n][*]=0. 3. Option 1: delete s[i] -> dp[i+1][k-1]. 4. Option 2: keep s[i]; scan j from i, same=count of s[i], del=count of others (deleted); if del<=k: cand = cost(same) + dp[j+1][k-del]. 5. Answer dp[0][k]. Confirm the exact cost model in the real statement.
dry_run: Own example: s=aaabcccd, k=2: delete b and d -> a3c3 -> length 4.

brief: Beauty of a subarray = its LIS length. Count ways to split the array into contiguous pieces whose beauties are strictly increasing left to right.
key_idea: Precompute LIS of every subarray (patience sorting per left end), then dp[i][b] = ways for prefix i whose last piece has beauty b, using prefix sums over b.
solution: 1. lis[l][r] for all l<=r: for each l run patience sorting extending r (O(n^2 log n)). 2. P[j][x] = number of ways to split prefix j with last beauty <= x; P[0][x]=1 for all x (empty prefix). 3. For each i and each j<i: b=lis[j+1][i]; dp_i[b] += P[j][b-1]. 4. Build P[i] as prefix sums of dp_i. Answer P[n][n] (mod 1e9+7 assumed). 5. Memory: store lis as short and P as int arrays (~2000x2000).
complexity: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space

brief: Circular pizza of 3n slices; choose exactly n slices maximizing total size. Adjacent chosen slices (circularly) are allowed only by spending one token per adjacent pair, at most K tokens.
key_idea: Linear DP dp[chosen][tokensUsed][lastChosen], run twice (first slice chosen or not) to handle the circular wrap pair.
solution: 1. Interpretation: count each adjacent chosen pair (including last-first) as one token; total pairs <= K. 2. Fix f = whether slice 0 is chosen. dp[c][t][last] = best sum over processed slices. 3. Slice i not chosen: last=0. Chosen: c+1, t += last (adjacent to previous chosen). 4. At the end, if f=1 and last=1 the wrap pair costs one more token; require c=n, t<=K. 5. Answer = max over both runs; -inf states skipped.
complexity: O(3n * n * K) time, O(n*K) space
dry_run: Sample n=1,K=0,[10,20,30]: choose one slice, no pairs -> best 30.

brief: Longest subsequence of prices where consecutive chosen prices differ by at least M and directions alternate up/down, allowing at most one place where the direction repeats.
key_idea: dp[i][dir][used] = longest valid subsequence ending at i with last move dir; transitions are prefix/suffix max queries over values, so use Fenwick trees on compressed prices.
solution: 1. dp[i][U][u]: last move was up into i (p[j] <= p[i]-M); dp[i][D][u]: down into i (p[j] >= p[i]+M); u = mulligan used (0/1). Base: a single element counts as 1 in every state. 2. dp[i][U][0] = 1 + max dp[j][D][0] over p[j] <= p[i]-M; dp[i][U][1] = 1 + max(dp[j][D][1], dp[j][U][0]) over same j. 3. Symmetric for D using p[j] >= p[i]+M (suffix max). 4. Keep 4 prefix-max BITs (for U-queries) and 4 suffix-max BITs (for D-queries) keyed by compressed price; process i left to right, query then insert. 5. Answer = max over all states (at least 1). Assumes M >= 1.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

20(last): down from 30: D1 = U1(30)+1 = 4 -> answer 4.

brief: Form the maximum number of disjoint triplets where each triplet is three equal numbers or three consecutive numbers (CF 1110D Jongmah).
key_idea: Never need 3+ identical consecutive runs from the same start; DP over values with the number of runs started at v-1 and v (0..2 each).
solution: 1. cnt[v] = number of tiles with value v. 2. dp[b][c] after processing value v: b = number of runs (v-1,v,v+1) started at v-1, c = runs (v,v+1,v+2) started at v; each kept <= 2 (3 equal runs can be replaced by triples of equal values). 3. Transition at value v with a = runs started at v-2, b = at v-1, choose c in 0..2 with a+b+c <= cnt[v]: ndp[b][c] = max(dp[a][b] + c + (cnt[v]-a-b-c)/3). 4. Process v = 1..M+2 (cnt=0 for v>M) so unfinished runs are forced to 0; answer dp[0][0]. 5. Runs are counted when started; leftover tiles of value v form equal triples.
complexity: O(27 * M + N) time, O(M) space

v=1: c=0 -> 0 (c>0 impossible later since cnt3=0 ends up invalid); v=2: leftover 3 twos -> 1 triple.

brief: N ingredients with 3 units each; M recipes given as binary strings (which ingredients they use, one unit each), each usable once with a price; maximize total price.
key_idea: 0/1 knapsack where the 'weight' is a vector of per-ingredient usage counts (0..3) encoded in base 4.
solution: 1. Encode usage state as base-4 number of N digits (digit = units used of that ingredient). 2. dp[state] = max price; dp[0]=0, others -inf. 3. For each recipe (copy dp first): for each reachable state, if every ingredient used by the recipe has digit < 3, new state = state + sum 4^j over its ingredients; update with price. 4. Answer = max dp. Feasible for N up to about 9-10 (4^N states); constraints were not given. 5. If N is large but M small, use bitmask over recipes and check counts instead.

brief: Given binary string Q (value X), count pairs (i,j) of non-negative integers with i+j <= X and i XOR j = X, mod 1e9+7 (statement as posted is ambiguous).
key_idea: i+j = (i XOR j) + 2*(i AND j) >= X, so i+j <= X forces i AND j = 0: every set bit of X goes to exactly one of i, j.
solution: 1. Identity: i + j = (i ^ j) + 2(i & j). With i^j = X, i+j <= X means i&j = 0 and i+j = X. 2. So each 1-bit of X is assigned to i or to j independently: ordered pairs = 2^c, c = number of '1's in Q. 3. Variants: unordered pairs 2^(c-1); excluding i=0 or j=0: 2^c - 2. 4. Compute pow(2,c) mod 1e9+7 (no digit DP needed for this reading).

brief: Split the array into exactly k segments; a segment's cost is the sum over distinct values of (last occurrence - first occurrence) inside it; minimize the total (CF 1527E).
key_idea: Segment cost = sum of (i - prev[i]) over i whose previous equal element is inside the segment; for each layer, adding i adds (i-prev[i]) to every split point j < prev[i] - a lazy range-add/range-min segment tree.
solution: 1. dp_k[i] = min over j<i of dp_{k-1}[j] + cost(j+1..i). 2. prev[i] = previous index with the same value (0 if none, 1-based). 3. For each layer build a segment tree over j=0..n holding dp_{k-1}[j]; sweep i=1..n: if prev[i]>0 add (i-prev[i]) on [0, prev[i]-1]; dp_k[i] = min on [0, i-1]. 4. Repeat k layers; answer dp_k[n]. Use INF for invalid states.
complexity: O(k * n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Array A, costs X (subtract 1 from every element of a chosen subarray) and Y (set one positive element to 0); minimum cost to make all zeros.
key_idea: CF 448C style divide and conquer: for each positive segment, min(Y*length, X*(min-base) + recurse on pieces split at the minimum).
solution: 1. f(l,r,base) for a segment whose elements are all > base. 2. Option A: Y*(r-l+1) (zero each element). 3. Option B: X*(m-base) where m = segment min, then split at positions equal to m and add f(piece, m). 4. f = min(A,B); answer = sum of f over maximal positive segments with base 0. 5. Sparse table for range min speeds it up; worst case O(n^2).
complexity: O(n^2) worst case time, O(n) space

brief: Count balanced bracket strings of length N that contain the given bracket string S as a subsequence (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: Greedy subsequence matching is canonical, so state = (position, balance, how much of S is matched).
solution: 1. dp[i][b][k] = number of prefixes of length i with balance b (never negative) that greedily matched the first k chars of S. 2. Append c in {'(' , ')'}: b' = b +/- 1 (skip if negative or > N-i-1 can't close); k' = k + (k<|S| and S[k]==c). 3. dp[0][0][0]=1; answer dp[N][0][|S|]. 4. Odd N -> 0. Roll the first dimension to save memory.

brief: N people, M days: exactly X[i] people get their first dose on day i, at most Y[i] get their second dose on day i, and the second dose is on or after the first-dose day. Count (first,second) day assignments to people mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Choose who gets first doses on each day (multinomial), then sweep days keeping the number of people still waiting for a second dose; on day i pick which s of them get it (C(p,s)).
solution: 1. First doses: N! / prod X[i]! ways. 2. dp[p] = ways with p people pending a second dose; start dp[0]=1. 3. Day i: p += X[i] (same-day second dose allowed); then for s = 0..min(Y[i],p): ndp[p-s] += dp[p] * C(p,s). 4. After day M, answer = multinomial * dp[0]. 5. Precompute factorials up to N for C and the multinomial.
complexity: O(M * N * maxY) time, O(N) space

Day1: p=1 -> s=0: dp[1]=1; s=1: dp[0]=1.
Day2: from p=1 -> p=3, need s<=2 so can't reach 0; from p=0 -> p=2, s=2: dp[0]=1.

brief: Count ordered ways (sequences) to make change W from N coin types with values A[i] <= 100 (unlimited use), W up to 1e9, modulo a prime.
key_idea: dp[w] = sum over v of cnt[v]*dp[w-v] is a linear recurrence of order 100, so raise its 100x100 companion matrix to the W-th power.
solution: 1. cnt[v] = number of coin types with value v (types with equal values still count separately). 2. dp[0]=1, dp[w] = sum_{v=1..100} cnt[v]*dp[w-v] (dp of negative index = 0). 3. Compute dp[0..99] directly; if W < 100 print dp[W]. 4. Else build companion matrix T (first row = cnt[1..100], subdiagonal ones), state vector (dp[99],...,dp[0]); result = T^(W-99) applied, first entry. 5. Mod 1e9+7 assumed.
complexity: O(100^3 log W) time, O(100^2) space

brief: Given array A (N<=1e5, A[i]<=100) and X<=1e9, count the ways (ordered sequences, unlimited reuse) to reach sum X; mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[w] = sum over v of cnt[v]*dp[w-v] is a linear recurrence of order 100, so raise its 100x100 companion matrix to the W-th power.
solution: 1. Order must matter (unordered counting is infeasible for X=1e9 with this many values), so ways[x] = sum_v cnt[v]*ways[x-v], cnt[v] = how many array elements equal v. 2. ways[0]=1; compute ways[0..99] directly. 3. For X>=100 use the 100x100 companion matrix raised to X-99 (matrix exponentiation). 4. If the array has duplicates and they should count once, set cnt[v]=1 for present values instead.
complexity: O(100^3 log W) time, O(100^2) space

brief: Split an array of gift types into K consecutive non-empty boxes maximizing the sum over boxes of the number of distinct types.
key_idea: Layered DP; when a[i] is appended, every split point j >= prev[i] gains +1 distinct - range add + range max (CF 833B).
solution: 1. dp_k[i] = max over j<i of dp_{k-1}[j] + distinct(j+1..i). 2. prev[i] = last index before i with the same type (0 if none). 3. For each layer: segment tree over j=0..n storing dp_{k-1}[j] (with -INF where invalid); sweeping i, a[i] is new for every split j in [prev[i], i-1] -> range add +1 there; dp_k[i] = max on [0,i-1]. 4. Run K layers; answer dp_K[n] (CF 833B The Bakery).
complexity: O(K * n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Count ways to split array A into contiguous pieces so that the sequence of piece MEX values is non-decreasing; answer modulo a given number.
key_idea: For a fixed right end, MEX of a[j..i] only grows as j moves left, so enumerate j while maintaining the mex; dp over (end, last mex) with prefix sums over mex.
solution: 1. P[j][m] = ways to split prefix j with last mex <= m; P[0][m]=1 for all m. 2. For each i: walk j from i down to 1, mark a[j] seen (ignore values > n), advance mex while seen[mex]. 3. dp_i[mex] += P[j-1][mex] (previous piece's mex must be <= this one). 4. P[i] = prefix sums of dp_i over m = 0..n+1; answer P[n][n+1] mod the given modulus. 5. Constraints not given; this is O(n^2) time and memory, fine up to n ~ 3000.

brief: Given N, M and values <= M, form the maximum number of disjoint triplets, each three equal numbers or three consecutive numbers (CF 1110D Jongmah).
key_idea: Never need 3+ identical consecutive runs from the same start; DP over values with the number of runs started at v-1 and v (0..2 each).
solution: 1. cnt[v] = number of tiles with value v. 2. dp[b][c] after processing value v: b = number of runs (v-1,v,v+1) started at v-1, c = runs (v,v+1,v+2) started at v; each kept <= 2 (3 equal runs can be replaced by triples of equal values). 3. Transition at value v with a = runs started at v-2, b = at v-1, choose c in 0..2 with a+b+c <= cnt[v]: ndp[b][c] = max(dp[a][b] + c + (cnt[v]-a-b-c)/3). 4. Process v = 1..M+2 (cnt=0 for v>M) so unfinished runs are forced to 0; answer dp[0][0]. 5. Runs are counted when started; leftover tiles of value v form equal triples.

brief: Partition the array into contiguous pieces of length >= K; a piece's beauty is the maximum XOR of any subset of its elements; maximize the total beauty.
key_idea: dp is non-decreasing for j >= K, and for a fixed end i the span of a[j+1..i] changes at most 17 times as j decreases; a position-tagged (latest-index) linear basis gives those change points and the max XOR for each.
solution: 1. dp[0]=0, dp[j]=-inf for 1<=j<K; dp[i] = max over j<=i-K of dp[j] + maxXor(a[j+1..i]). 2. Maintain a linear basis over prefix a[1..i] where each slot keeps the vector with the LATEST position (swap when inserting a newer one). Vectors with pos > j form a basis of a[j+1..i]. 3. Candidate j's: i-K, min(pos_b - 1, i-K) for each basis slot, and 0. Within a block of equal span, the largest valid j is best since dp is non-decreasing for j>=K. 4. For each candidate (j==0 or j>=K), greedy max XOR using slots with pos > j (from high bit: res=max(res,res^v)). 5. Answer dp[n].

Answer = sum over end states of (T^N)[start=0][end]. 4. Matrix size up to 201 -> 201^3 * 30 is about 2.4e8 operations, acceptable. 5. Verify the real condition before using.

brief: Implement a Disjoint Set Union with make_set, find_set (path compression) and union_sets, and explain union by size/rank.
key_idea: Each set is a tree with a root representative; path compression flattens trees and union by size keeps them shallow, giving near-constant amortized time.
solution: 1. make_set(v): parent[v]=v, size[v]=1. 2. find_set(v): if parent[v]==v return v; else parent[v]=find_set(parent[v]) (path compression). 3. union_sets(a,b): a=find(a), b=find(b); if equal return; attach smaller-size root under larger; size[a]+=size[b]. 4. Union by rank is the same idea using tree height estimates; both together give O(alpha(n)) amortized. 5. Only path compression: O(log n) amortized; neither: O(n) worst case chains.
complexity: O(alpha(n)) amortized per operation, O(n) space

brief: n nodes; queries either add edge (i,j) or ask how many maximal runs of consecutive labels make up u's component; output the sum of all answers.
key_idea: runs(component) = size - (number of pairs (x, x+1) both in the component); maintain that pair count during small-to-large merges.
solution: 1. DSU with member lists; pairs[root] = count of x with x and x+1 in the same component. 2. Union(a,b): roots ra, rb (rb smaller). For each x in rb's list, count x-1 and x+1 whose root is ra -> cross. 3. pairs[ra] = pairs[ra] + pairs[rb] + cross; move rb's members into ra; size adds. 4. Ask u: r=find(u), answer size[r] - pairs[r]; add to the total (use long long). 5. Count cross before changing parents.
complexity: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Robot on an n x m elevation grid moves up/down/left/right only to strictly higher cells; find the maximum number of cells in such a path starting anywhere (Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix).
key_idea: Strictly increasing moves form a DAG; dp[cell] = 1 + max dp of higher neighbours, computed by memoized DFS or in decreasing height order.
solution: 1. Sort cells by height descending (avoids deep recursion). 2. dp[c] = 1 + max(dp[nb]) over 4-neighbours nb with height[nb] > height[c]; all higher cells are already final. 3. Answer = max dp. 4. Equal heights never connect (strictly higher only). 5. Memoized DFS is the usual interview form; same complexity.
complexity: O(nm log(nm)) time with sorting (O(nm) with memo DFS), O(nm) space

solution: 1. Assumption (statement vague): discard edges with weight < K; path length = sum of weights (or edge count). 2. Topological order via Kahn's algorithm on the remaining edges. 3. dp[v] = max(0, max over edges u->v of dp[u] + w) - paths may start anywhere. 4. Answer = max dp[v]. 5. If the threshold means 'minimum edge on the path >= K' it is the same filter.
complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space

brief: TOR of two ternary numbers is digit-wise (x+y) mod 3. Given n and ternary string c, find two n-digit ternary numbers a, b without leading zeros with TOR(a,b)=c minimizing max(a,b); print it mod 1e9+7 (or -1).
key_idea: Keep a and b equal as long as possible; at the first digit that forces a difference, give the 1 to a and from then on a gets all 0s while b takes c's digits.
solution: 1. Digit 0: (0,0) while equal; digit 2: (1,1); digit 1: (1,0) -> a becomes larger (split). 2. First digit (no leading zeros): c=2 -> (1,1); c=1 -> (2,2); c=0 -> (2,1) and split. 3. After the split: a gets 0 and b gets c[i] for every later digit (keeps the larger one as small as possible). 4. max(a,b)=a; print its digit string read as a decimal number mod 1e9+7 (sample 22 -> 11 shows digits are printed as is). 5. A valid pair always exists for n>=1, so -1 never actually happens.

brief: Digit string A (digits 1-9) and mapping F; at most once replace every digit of one contiguous segment by F[digit]. Output the maximum resulting number mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Start at the first digit that strictly increases, continue while the mapping does not decrease (CF 1157B).
solution: 1. Lexicographic greedy: the leftmost position where F[d] > d should start the segment (earlier digits matter most). 2. From there keep replacing while F[d] >= d (equal digits don't hurt and let the segment continue). 3. Stop at the first digit with F[d] < d. 4. If no digit has F[d] > d, do nothing. 5. Print the resulting number mod 1e9+7 (Horner's rule over digits).
dry_run: Own example: A=1337, F(1)=1, F(3)=5, F(7)=3, others identity: skip '1' (equal), start at '3'->5, '3'->5, stop at '7' (3<7) -> 1557.

brief: N students, halls A and B each holding N/2; hallA[i], hallB[i] are times for student i. Assign everyone to minimize total time.
key_idea: Exchange argument: sort by A[i]-B[i]; the half with the smallest difference goes to A (Two City Scheduling).
solution: 1. Imagine everyone goes to hall B; moving student i to A changes the total by A[i]-B[i]. 2. Pick the N/2 students with the smallest A[i]-B[i] for hall A, the rest for B. 3. Sorting by difference is O(N log N); nth_element gives O(N) average. 4. Total = sum of B + sum of the chosen differences.
complexity: O(N) average with nth_element (O(N log N) with sort), O(N) space

brief: 2N packages split N to center A and N to center B; package i costs A_i at A and min(A_i,B_i)+B_i at B. Minimize total cost.
key_idea: Same as two-city scheduling after computing the effective B cost: sort by effB - A.
solution: 1. Effective cost to B: effB[i] = min(A[i],B[i]) + B[i]. 2. Start with everyone in A: total = sum A. 3. Moving item i to B adds effB[i]-A[i]; exactly N must move. 4. Sort the differences and add the N smallest (exchange argument). 5. Use long long for sums.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

brief: 2n employees go to cities A and B, n each; cost to A is direct, cost to B is min(costA,costB)+costB via a transit hub. Minimize total cost.
key_idea: Compute effective B cost, send everyone to A, then move the n people with the smallest (effB - A) to B.
solution: 1. Effective cost to B: effB[i] = min(A[i],B[i]) + B[i]. 2. Start with everyone in A: total = sum A. 3. Moving item i to B adds effB[i]-A[i]; exactly N must move. 4. Sort the differences and add the N smallest (exchange argument). 5. Use long long for sums.

brief: In one step remove two elements with different values, or a single element. Minimum steps to empty the array.
key_idea: Answer = max(maxFrequency, ceil(n/2)).
solution: 1. Each step removes at most 2 elements -> at least ceil(n/2) steps. 2. Copies of the most frequent value can never be removed together -> at least maxFreq steps. 3. Both bounds are achievable: repeatedly pair the most frequent value with another value (priority queue argument), so answer = max(maxFreq, ceil(n/2)). 4. Count frequencies with a hash map; no sorting needed.

brief: Array where each element is the maximum jump length from that index; find the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index.
key_idea: BFS by levels in O(n): track the farthest reach of the current jump window; when you pass the window end, take a jump.
solution: 1. jumps=0, curEnd=0, far=0. 2. For i in 0..n-2: far = max(far, i+a[i]); if i==curEnd: jumps++, curEnd=far; if curEnd <= i, unreachable (-1). 3. Answer jumps (n==1 -> 0). 4. GfG version: return -1 if the end can't be reached (e.g. a[0]=0 and n>1).
dry_run: Own example: [2,3,1,1,4]: i=0 far=2, jump1 end=2; i=1 far=4; i=2 end reached -> jump2 end=4 -> 2.

brief: Petrol pumps on a circle with petrol amount and distance to the next pump; find the first pump from which a truck can complete the tour (GfG Circular Tour), or -1.
key_idea: Gas station greedy: reset the start whenever the running surplus goes negative; feasible iff total surplus >= 0.
solution: 1. If total gas < total cost, no start works -> -1. 2. Scan with a running tank; when the tank becomes negative at i, no start in [start..i] works, so set start=i+1 and reset tank. 3. The final start is the answer when total >= 0. 4. One pass, no need to simulate from every start.

solution: 1. Count matches, p = #(A=1,B=0), q = #(A=0,B=1). 2. Each useful swap exchanges one p-position with one q-position, gaining 2 matches. 3. Answer = matches + 2*min(K, p, q). 4. If swaps are adjacent-only or across arrays, the model changes - confirm the statement.

brief: Buy any two items and get a third free if its cost is <= the cheaper of the two; at most V items can be free. Minimize the total cost to collect all items.
key_idea: Sort descending; the k-th free item can be at most the 3k-th largest price, and taking exactly a[3], a[6], ... (first V of them) achieves that bound.
solution: 1. Sort prices in descending order (1-based a1 >= a2 >= ...). 2. Free items: a[3], a[6], ..., a[3k] for k = 1..min(V, n/3) (each paired with the two items just before it). 3. Answer = total sum - sum of those free items. 4. Proof: the k-th largest free item needs 2k paid + k free items >= it, so it is <= a[3k]. 5. Reported N,V <= 1e9 is unrealistic for reading input; treat n as array size and cap V by n/3.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space

brief: Arrange non-negative integers (given as strings) so their concatenation is the largest possible number; return it as a string.
key_idea: Sort with comparator a+b > b+a (this ordering is transitive).

brief: Given a list of digits and at most K swaps (any two positions), produce the smallest possible number using all digits.
key_idea: At each position, if a smaller digit exists to the right, swap in the minimum - but try every occurrence of that minimum (picking one occurrence greedily can be wrong).
solution: 1. solve(idx, k): record s if better than best; stop if k==0 or idx==n. 2. mn = smallest digit in s[idx+1..]. If mn >= s[idx], move on: solve(idx+1, k) (no swap spent). 3. Else for every j > idx with s[j]==mn: swap(s[idx], s[j]), solve(idx+1, k-1), swap back. 4. Exponential worst case but fine for typical small inputs; if the number may not start with 0, skip mn='0' at idx 0. 5. Pure greedy (rightmost min) fails e.g. for the max version on 4399 style inputs with duplicates.
complexity: O(n * branches^k) worst case, O(n) recursion
dry_run: Own example: 9 1 3 1, K=2: idx0: min 1 at j=1 or 3; j=3 -> 1 1 3 9 (then idx1 already min) -> 1139; j=1 -> 1 9 3 1 -> swap 9 with last 1 -> 1139. Best 1139.

brief: M heroes each with health H fight N villains in order; hero with health X vs villain V: X>V -> villain dies, hero has X-V; X==V -> both die; X<V -> hero dies. Remove the minimum number of villains from the front so the rest can be defeated by at most M heroes.
key_idea: The remaining villains form a suffix; fewer villains never need more heroes, so binary search the smallest number removed and simulate.
solution: 1. simulate(s): heroes fight villains s..N-1 in order; when the current hero dies call the next one; fail if more than M heroes are needed. 2. Assume when a hero loses the villain keeps its full health (as stated); if the real rule reduces the villain to V-X, change one line. 3. Monotonic: removing more front villains never hurts -> binary search s in [0, N]. 4. Answer = smallest feasible s. 5. A villain with V >= H can only be killed by a tie (V == H).
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(1) extra space

brief: n rods with length and material 0/1; pair a material-0 rod with a material-1 rod (each used at most once); pair value = min length. Maximize the total, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Sort each material descending and pair them rank by rank; take min(c0,c1) pairs (values are positive).
solution: 1. Split lengths by material. 2. Sort both lists descending. 3. Pair i-th with i-th for i < min(c0,c1); add min(x[i], y[i]). 4. Exchange argument: pairing large with large never lowers the sum of mins. 5. Sum in long long, print mod 1e9+7.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Rearrange a string so that no two adjacent characters are equal; output -1 if impossible.
key_idea: Possible iff maxFreq <= ceil(n/2); place characters by decreasing frequency at even indices 0,2,4,... then odd ones.
solution: 1. Count frequencies; if maxFreq > (n+1)/2 print -1. 2. Order characters by frequency (most frequent first). 3. Fill positions 0,2,4,...; when past the end, continue at 1,3,5,... 4. The most frequent char fills only even slots, so no equal neighbours appear. 5. Priority-queue alternative: always place the most frequent char different from the previous one.

brief: Minimum number of adjacent swaps so that all even values are on one side and all odd values on the other.
key_idea: Relative order inside each parity never needs to change, so moving evens to the left costs sum(pos_k - k) over the k-th even; compute both orientations and take the min.
solution: 1. cost(evens left) = sum over evens (k-th even, 0-based) of (index - k). 2. cost(odds left) = same formula over odd values. 3. Answer = min of the two (each adjacent swap of an even-odd pair moves one element one step). 4. Use long long (up to ~2.5e9).

brief: N passengers with fares; groups of at most K passengers all pay the group's minimum fare (group pays size x min fare). Find the maximum total saving from grouping.
key_idea: Use g = ceil(N/K) groups; their leaders (minimums) should be the g cheapest fares, with the biggest groups (size K) given to the cheapest leaders.
solution: 1. Sort fares ascending f1 <= f2 <= ...; g = ceil(N/K). 2. Payment = K*(f1+...+f_{g-1}) + (N - K*(g-1)) * f_g; other passengers can join any leader since they are all >= the leaders. 3. More groups never helps: splitting someone out makes them pay their own (higher) fare. 4. Saving = sum of all fares - payment. 5. Note: grouping need not be consecutive in sorted order (fares 1,2,3, K=2: {1,3},{2} saves 2).
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(1) extra space

brief: Array A of N elements; choose M elements, beauty = their sum, and each second beauty increases by M. Find the minimum time for beauty to reach X (statement ambiguous).
key_idea: For a fixed M the best start is the M largest elements; try every M and take the minimum ceil((X - S_M)/M).
solution: 1. Sort A descending; prefix sums S_m = sum of top m. 2. For each m in 1..N: if S_m >= X time 0, else time = ceil((X - S_m)/m). 3. Answer = min over m. 4. N <= 100 so this is trivial; values fit in long long.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(1) extra space

brief: Children in a line with ratings; each gets at least one candy and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more than that neighbour. Minimize total candies.
key_idea: Two passes: left-to-right enforces the left neighbour rule, right-to-left the right one; take the max at each child.
solution: 1. c[i]=1 for all. 2. Left pass: if r[i] > r[i-1], c[i] = c[i-1]+1. 3. Right pass: if r[i] > r[i+1], c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1]+1). 4. Answer = sum c. 5. Equal neighbours have no constraint.

brief: N posts; a lamp on post i lights i-1, i, i+1; dead posts 'D' cannot hold lamps but must be lit; one optional generator truck lights a post and its neighbours for free. Minimize lamps or -1.
key_idea: Prefix DP (min lamps to light the first j posts) + suffix DP; the truck removes one window of 3, so combine prefix and suffix around it.
solution: 1. c[j] = min lamps to light positions [0, j) using lamps on 'L' posts: last needed post j-1 is lit by a lamp at p in {j-2, j-1, j} (p must be 'L'), so c[j] = min c[max(0,p-1)] + 1; c[0]=0. 2. d[j] = min lamps to light [j, n): same DP on the reversed string. 3. No truck: c[n]. Truck at t lights [t-1, t+1]: c[max(0,t-1)] + d[min(n,t+2)] (left and right parts can't share a lamp since they are 4 apart). 4. Answer = min over all options; INF -> -1. 5. Lamps may stand on any 'L' post; dead posts only need to be lit.

brief: Array of even length where each value appears exactly twice; minimum adjacent swaps so every equal pair becomes adjacent.
key_idea: Greedy (CF 995B): take the first element, bring its partner next to it with adjacent swaps, remove both, repeat.
solution: 1. While the list is non-empty: x = v[0]; find j > 0 with v[j] == x. 2. Add j-1 swaps (move partner left to index 1), erase both. 3. Exchange argument: fixing the leftmost element's pair first never costs extra. 4. O(n^2) with vector erase; use a BIT over positions for O(n log n) if n is large.

brief: N segments with levels L[i]; on day D any chosen segments can be lowered by 2D-1. Find the minimum number of days to make L strictly decreasing.
key_idea: After d days a segment can be lowered by any sum of distinct odd numbers 1..2d-1, i.e. any value in [0, d^2] except 2 and d^2-2; binary search d and greedily keep each segment as high as possible.
solution: 1. Achievable reductions with d days: 0..d^2 except 2 and d^2-2 (d=1: only {0,1}). 2. Check(d): left to right, need_i = max(0, L_i - (prev - 1)) (first segment need 0); pick the smallest achievable r >= need_i (need==2 or d^2-2 -> need+1); fail if r > d^2; prev = L_i - r. 3. Greedy is optimal: keeping each level as high as possible only loosens later constraints. 4. Binary search smallest feasible d in [0, 1e5] (needed reductions are below ~2.1e9). 5. The note's ceil(sqrt(max need)) is almost right but misses the unreachable totals 2 and d^2-2.
complexity: O(N log maxD) time, O(1) extra space

Own example [3,3,3]: needs 0,1,2 -> d=2 gives r=3 for the third (2 unreachable) -> levels 3,2,0 -> 2.

brief: Binary string ('ugliness' = its binary value); with a CASH budget you may swap two characters for cost A or flip one bit for cost B; minimize the final value.
key_idea: Higher bits dominate: for each possible number of flips f, remove the top ones (flips + useful swaps into the lowest zeros) and keep the lexicographically smallest result.
solution: 1. Exact rules unclear (swap any two positions vs adjacent); assume any two positions. 2. Simple greedy (always use the cheaper operation on the highest 1) can fail: s=10, A=1, B=2, CASH=2 - swapping gives 01 but flipping gives 00. 3. Enumerate f = number of flips (f*B <= CASH); w = number of swaps with the rest of the money. 4. With f, w: clear the top f+w ones; the w swapped ones land on the rightmost original zeros (only while the landing zero is to the right of the source one); build the string and keep the minimum. 5. O(n^2) overall; verify on the sample and the real constraints.
dry_run: Sample 011111, CASH=7, A=1, B=3: the only zero is the MSB, so swaps are useless; f=2 flips (cost 6) -> 000111 = 7.

brief: Make the array all zeros using 'subtract 1 from a subarray' (cost X) or 'set one element to zero' (cost Y); minimize the cost.
key_idea: CF 448C style divide and conquer: for each positive segment, min(Y*length, X*(min-base) + recurse on pieces split at the minimum).
solution: 1. f(l,r,base) for a segment whose elements are all > base. 2. Option A: Y*(r-l+1) (zero each element). 3. Option B: X*(m-base) where m = segment min, then split at positions equal to m and add f(piece, m). 4. f = min(A,B); answer = sum of f over maximal positive segments with base 0. 5. Sparse table for range min speeds it up; worst case O(n^2).
complexity: O(n^2) worst case time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Listed sample N=3,X=2,Y=3,[4,2,1] -> 8.
Recursion: A=9; B = 2*1 + f([4,2],base1): min(6, 2*1 + min(3, 2*2)=5) = 5 -> 7.
Sequence: subtract all once (2) -> [3,1,0]; subtract [3,1] once (2) -> [2,0,0]; zero the 2 (3) = 7 < 8, so the listed 8 seems wrong (or the rules differ).

brief: N food types: buying food i the first time gives v[i] taste, each repeat gives d[i] less than the previous one. Buy up to M meals to maximize total taste.
key_idea: Take the M largest positive terms from all arithmetic sequences; binary search the threshold value T and sum each sequence's terms >= T with the AP formula.
solution: 1. cnt(T) = sum over i with v[i] >= T of floor((v[i]-T)/d[i]) + 1 (cap at M+1; assumes d[i] >= 1). 2. Binary search the smallest T >= 1 with cnt(T) <= M. 3. Take all terms >= T (AP sums: k terms starting at v with step d: k*v - d*k*(k-1)/2). 4. Fill remaining M - cnt(T) slots with value T-1 if T-1 >= 1 (there are enough of them since cnt(T-1) > M). 5. Non-positive tastes are never bought (buying is optional). Use __int128 or careful long long.
complexity: O(N log V) time, O(1) extra space

brief: Perform at most k swaps between any array elements to maximize the maximum subarray sum (n <= 500, k <= 1e9).
key_idea: Fix the subarray [l,r]; the best k swaps exchange its smallest elements with the largest outside elements while that improves the sum (CF 425A).
solution: 1. For each l, keep 'inside' sorted ascending and 'outside' sorted descending; extend r one by one (insert a[r] into inside, remove it from outside). 2. For the current [l,r]: sum = inside sum; for t < min(k, |inside|, |outside|): if outside[t] > inside[t], sum += outside[t]-inside[t], else stop. 3. Track the maximum over all (l,r). 4. k >= n is effectively n. 5. O(n) per (l,r) -> O(n^3) = 1.25e8 simple ops for n=500.
dry_run: Own example: [1,-5,3], k=1: subarray [1,-5] swap -5 with 3 -> 1+3 = 4; whole array sum -1 swap? no outside. Best 4.

brief: Make levels strictly decreasing; on day D any chosen segments can be lowered by 2^(D-1). Find the minimum number of days.
key_idea: After d days any reduction 0..2^d-1 is possible (binary representation), so compute the minimal needed reduction greedily and take the smallest d with 2^d - 1 >= max need.
solution: 1. Left to right: first segment keeps its level; for i>0 need = max(0, L[i] - (prev - 1)), prev = L[i] - need. 2. Lowering exactly 'need' is best (keeps later constraints loose). 3. maxNeed = max over all needs; answer = smallest d with 2^d - 1 >= maxNeed (0 if maxNeed = 0). 4. maxNeed can exceed 2e9 -> use long long.

brief: Songs have coefficients A[i]; when played with volume V the loudness A[i]*V must lie in [X,Y]. Find the minimum number of times V must change to play all songs in order.
key_idea: Each song allows V in [ceil(X/A), floor(Y/A)]; greedily keep the intersection of consecutive intervals and change V only when it becomes empty.
solution: 1. Interval for song i (A>0, integer V assumed): lo = ceil(X/A[i]), hi = floor(Y/A[i]); if lo > hi print -1. 2. cur = interval of song 0; for each next song intersect; if empty, changes++ and cur = that song's interval. 3. Answer = changes (setting the initial V is not counted). 4. Greedy is optimal: extending the current segment as far as possible never hurts (classic interval stabbing). 5. If V may be real, use real intervals [X/A, Y/A] instead.
